hook: Inuit communities in the Canadian Arctic live thousands of kilometers from any farm or factory. Yet tests in the 1980s and 1990s found some of the highest levels of certain pesticides and industrial chemicals in the world in their blood and breast milk. The chemicals had traveled north on the wind and up the food chain into the seals and whales people ate.

ideas: A persistent organic pollutant (POP) is a synthetic, carbon-based chemical that resists breakdown, dissolves in fat, travels long distances and is toxic.
Examples: DDT and other old pesticides, PCBs from electrical equipment, and dioxins from burning plastics and some industrial processes.
POPs collect in cold regions far from where they were used, and they are stored in fat, so they build up in animals over time.
Harm: thin eggshells (DDT in birds of prey), reproductive and immune problems, some cancers. The Stockholm Convention (2001) restricts them worldwide.

misconception.wrong: Once a chemical is banned, it soon disappears from the environment.
misconception.right: A POP breaks down so slowly that it stays in soil, sediment and animal fat for decades after it is banned, falling only gradually.

summary: Persistent organic pollutants are synthetic, carbon-based chemicals such as DDT, PCBs and dioxins that resist breakdown, dissolve in fat, travel long distances on wind and water and stay toxic for decades. They collect in cold regions and in animal fat, harming reproduction and development; DDT thinned the eggshells of birds of prey. Bans such as the Stockholm Convention cut new inputs, but levels fall slowly.
